summary: An annotated list of the 100 RFCs numbered 3500 through 3599, serving as a status report on them. It is informational.

subtitle: Annotated summary of RFCs 3500 through 3599, with brief descriptions of each.

tldr.problem: A large body of RFCs has been published, each serving different purposes and maturity levels. Readers need an overview of what was produced in one hundred-RFC block to understand the landscape and find relevant documents.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3599 provides a single-page annotation for each RFC in the 3500-3599 range, listing the RFC number, author, publication date, title, and a 1-3 sentence plain-language summary of its purpose. RFCs on the standards track are marked.
tldr.outcome: The summary serves as a navigation aid and status report, helping readers understand the breadth of work undertaken in this RFC series. Standards-track RFCs cover IP, multimedia, security, management, and protocols; informational RFCs document requirements, architectures, and interim specifications.

today: RFC 3599 is an Informational index. The RFCs it summarizes have evolved in status over the years. Several have become Internet Standards, some have been obsoleted or updated, and others remain in force. Readers interested in a specific RFC from this range should check the current RFC status document for its present maturity level.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3599 is an index of RFCs numbered 3500 through 3599, published in December 2003. Each entry provides the RFC number, author(s), publication date, title, and a brief description of the document's content. The purpose is to serve as a status report and navigation aid for the Internet technical community, allowing readers to quickly understand what work was undertaken in this hundred-RFC block and locate documents relevant to their interests.

The RFC notes that many of these RFCs are on the standards track (Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, or Full Standard), while others are Informational, Experimental, or Best Current Practice. The precise status of each RFC may change over time, so readers should consult the latest edition of 'Internet Official Protocol Standards' for current maturity levels. RFCs on the standards track are explicitly marked in the summary.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo lists 100 RFCs with one- or two-sentence summaries of what each one does. It helps you find what you are looking for in a big collection of documents.

sections.title: Standards Track Documents
sections.content:
The RFC series from 3500 to 3599 contains numerous standards-track documents covering networking protocols and technologies. Notable examples include RFC 3550 (RTP: A Transport Protocol for Real-Time Applications) and RFC 3551 (RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences), which define the core real-time transport protocol and its profile for multimedia. RFC 3588 specifies the Diameter Base Protocol for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) services, a widely-deployed alternative to RADIUS. RFC 3596 defines DNS extensions for IPv6 address resolution, enabling the Domain Name System to support modern IP version 6 deployments.

Other standards-track documents address cryptography and security: RFC 3566 specifies the AES-XCBC-MAC algorithm for use with IPsec, RFC 3565 covers Advanced Encryption Standard usage in Cryptographic Message Syntax, and RFC 3560 describes RSA encryption key transport for CMS. Network management documents include RFC 3592 (SONET/SDH managed objects) and RFC 3591 (Optical Interface Type managed objects). Routing and policy documents comprise RFC 3564 (Differentiated Services-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering Requirements) and RFC 3586 (IPsec Policy Requirements). Protocol extensions include RFC 3581 (SIP rport parameter for NAT traversal) and RFC 3598 (Sieve mail filtering subaddress extension).

Many of these standards represent evolution and refinement of existing protocols, while others introduce new mechanisms. Collectively, they address the breadth of Internet infrastructure: multimedia transport, network security, management, routing, and application-level protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: This range of RFCs has many standards for real things networks actually use: voice and video protocols, encryption, domain name service, email filtering, network management, and routing.

sections.title: Informational and Experimental Documents
sections.content:
The range also contains many informational RFCs that document requirements, architectures, and prior art without specifying standards. RFC 3583 (Requirements of a Quality of Service Solution for Mobile IP) identifies requirements for QoS mechanisms to work with mobile devices. RFC 3549 (Linux Netlink as an IP Services Protocol) describes the Linux kernel's intra-kernel messaging and kernel-userspace communication protocol, serving as prior art for the ForCES working group. RFC 3582 (Goals for IPv6 Site-Multihoming Architectures) outlines goals for solving IPv6 site multihoming, without proposing a solution.

Other informational documents cover management and operations: RFC 3535 summarizes an IAB workshop on network management, RFC 3577 provides an introduction to the Remote Monitoring (RMON) family of MIB modules, and RFC 3575 describes IANA considerations for RADIUS. Documentation RFCs include RFC 3531 (IPv6 address assignment methods), RFC 3539 (AAA Transport Profile), and RFC 3541 (URN namespace for Web3D Consortium resources).

Experimental RFCs explore emerging or niche technologies: RFC 3561 (AODV Routing for Ad Hoc Networks) defines routing for mobile ad hoc networks, RFC 3529 (XML-RPC over BEEP) specifies RPC over the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol, and RFC 3528 (Mesh-enhanced Service Location Protocol) describes an extension to SLP. These documents serve to capture work in progress and establish a record of ideas explored.
sections.plainLanguage: Many RFCs here explain problems and list requirements (like QoS for phones), describe how things are built (like Linux networking), or explore experimental ideas. They are not standards yet, but they help guide future work.

sections.title: Technical Coverage and Themes
sections.content:
The 100 RFCs in this range cover a diverse set of technical areas. Real-time communication and multimedia protocols are prominent: beyond RTP (3550, 3551), RFC 3556 extends SDP for RTCP bandwidth, RFC 3558 specifies RTP payload format for voice codecs, and RFC 3525 defines the Megaco/H.248 gateway control protocol for media gateways. Cryptography and security span from key exchange (RFC 3526: MODP Groups for IKE) to message authentication (RFC 3537: HMAC key wrapping) to protocol specifications (RFC 3554: SCTP with IPsec).

Internet services and infrastructure protocols include RFC 3596 (DNS IPv6), RFC 3530 (NFS version 4), and RFC 3519 (Mobile IP NAT Traversal). Routing and QoS cover RFC 3567 (IS-IS authentication), RFC 3580 (802.1X RADIUS), RFC 3583 (Mobile IP QoS), and RFC 3564 (DiffServ-aware MPLS TE). Management and monitoring span RFC 3591-3593 (MIB modules for optical, SONET, and performance data), RFC 3559 (Multicast Address Allocation MIB), and RFC 3584 (SNMPv1/v2/v3 coexistence).

Special-purpose and application protocols include RFC 3533 (Ogg Encapsulation), RFC 3578 (ISUP-to-SIP mapping), RFC 3587 (IPv6 address allocation historic), and RFC 3597 (Handling unknown DNS RR types). Policy and security architecture RFCs (3520, 3521, 3585, 3586) address session authorization and IPsec policy. Taken together, these 100 RFCs represent a snapshot of the Internet standards and exploration landscape in 2003.
sections.plainLanguage: This range covers many network jobs: voice and video, encryption, internet services, routing, management, and specialized protocols. Together they show what the Internet community was working on in 2003.
